topic: Windows vs Chrome: The Browser Takeover
description: How Google Chrome and Chromium changed the browser market—while Microsoft’s Edge/legacy Internet Explorer lost share, users, and relevance across the 2010s.
youtube_description:
🚀 **Browser wars in slow motion**—and the winner was Google Chrome.

In this timeline comparison, we visualize how Chrome went from a niche browser to the global default while Microsoft’s legacy Internet Explorer collapsed, Edge had to reinvent itself, and Firefox steadily bled share.

**Chapters (timestamp-style):**
00:00 — 2009: Internet Explorer dominates (over 60%) while Chrome is barely on the map.
01:10 — 2011–2013: Chrome’s speed + Google integration begin the acceleration.
02:25 — 2014: Chrome crosses the “serious competitor” line.
03:40 — 2015–2016: The pivot era—Edge emerges, but IE still drags.
05:00 — 2017: Chrome becomes the clear #1 browser; Firefox keeps sliding.
06:10 — 2018–2020: IE ends up a legacy artifact; Edge starts gaining again (especially post-Chromium era).
07:20 — 2021–2026: Chrome stabilizes at ~high-60s share; Safari remains resilient; Firefox becomes a small-but-known player.

📌 **What to watch in the chart race:** the steep fall of Internet Explorer, the mid-pack climb of Edge, and Chrome’s long, dramatic “stair-step” takeover.

instagram_caption:
🚀 Chrome didn’t just “enter” the browser market—it *replaced* the default.

Back in 2009, the internet felt like Microsoft’s territory. **Internet Explorer sat at ~61.3% share**, while **Chrome was only ~2.2%**—basically a rounding error. Meanwhile **Firefox (~27.1%)** and **Safari (~9.8%)** were the other main players, shaping how people experienced the web day-to-day.

Then the turning point hit in the early 2010s. As Chrome’s performance and modern web engine approach spread, its share climbed fast: **2011 (~8.2%) → 2012 (~13.1%) → 2013 (~20.1%)**. By 2014, Chrome wasn’t just growing—it was *compounding*: **~28.3%**, while IE had already fallen to **~18.4%**. That’s the first dramatic squeeze—users switching because speed + stability started to feel better than tradition.

Microsoft tried to fight back with two moves: Edge arrives (initially from near-zero) and Internet Explorer keeps slipping. But the real storyline is the collapse of legacy trust. Look at the drop: **IE ~11.1% in 2015 → ~8.0% in 2016 → ~3.3% in 2018 → ~1.3% in 2020 → ~0.1% by 2024**. Meanwhile Edge begins to matter more: **~6.5% (2016) → ~11.6% (2018) → ~13.1% (2024)**.

By 2026, the chart is almost unfair: **Chrome holds ~69.8%**. **Firefox fades to ~3.4%**, and **Safari steadies around ~14%**. Chrome became the platform.

💬 **Question for you:** If you were a user back in the IE era, what made you switch first—speed, extensions, compatibility, or something else?

facebook_caption:
In this timeline comparison, we track global browser market share from 2009 through 2026 to show how the modern web consolidated under one platform.

In 2009, Internet Explorer led with approximately **61.3%** share, while Google Chrome was at about **2.2%**. Over the next decade, Chrome’s share rose steadily—**20.1% in 2013**, **28.3% in 2014**, and then a decisive climb into dominance—reaching **~60.2% by 2018**.

The inflection is most visible in Internet Explorer’s decline. IE drops from **~18.4% (2014)** to **~3.3% (2018)** and approaches near-removal levels—**~1.3% in 2020**, **~0.1% by 2024**, and effectively **0.0% by 2026**. Microsoft’s Edge begins later and experiences a slower ramp: starting from **~0% in early years**, then reaching **~11.6% in 2018** and **~13.1% by 2024**, reflecting a transition away from legacy.

Firefox declines across the period (**~27.1% in 2009 → ~3.4% by 2026**), while Safari remains comparatively resilient, hovering around the mid-teens (**~14% by 2026**).

Overall, the competitive story is clear: Chrome’s sustained adoption created a market gravity effect, while IE’s aging stack failed to keep users engaged.
